title: Ask HN: I’m an FCC Commissioner proposing regulation of IoT security updates
body:
Hi everyone, I’m FCC Commissioner Nathan Simington, and I’m here to discuss security updates for IoT devices and how you can make a difference by filing comments with the FCC.

As you know, serious vulnerabilities are common in IoT, and it often takes too long for these to be patched on end-user devices—if the manufacturer even bothers to release an update, and if the device was even designed to receive them. Companies may stop supporting a device well before consumers have stopped using it. The support period is often not communicated at the time of sale. And sometimes the end of support is not even announced, leaving even informed users unsure whether their devices are still safe.

I’ve advocated for the FCC to require device manufacturers to support their devices with security updates for a reasonable amount of time [1]. I can't bring such a proposal to a vote since I’m not the chairman of the agency. But I was able to convince my colleagues to tentatively support something a little more moderate addressing this problem.

The FCC recently issued a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking [2] for a cybersecurity labeling program for connected devices. If they meet certain criteria for the security of their product, manufacturers can put an FCC cybersecurity label on it. I fought hard for one of these criteria to be the disclosure of how long the product will receive security updates. I hope that, besides arming consumers with better information, the commitments on this label (including the support period) will be legally enforceable in contract and tort lawsuits and under other laws. You can see my full statement here [3].

But it’s too early to declare victory. Many manufacturers oppose making any commitments about security updates, even voluntary ones. title: Ask HN: I'm a software engineer going blind, how should I prepare?
body:
I'm a 24 y/o full stack engineer (I know some of you are rolling your eyes right now, just highlighting that I have experience on frontend apps as well as backend architecture). I've been working professionally for ~7 years building mostly javascript projects but also some PHP. Two years ago I was diagnosed with a condition called "Usher's Syndrome" - characterized by hearing loss, balance issues, and progressive vision loss.

I know there are blind software engineers out there. My main questions are:

- Are there blind frontend engineers?

- What kinds of software engineering lend themselves to someone with limited vision? Backend only?

- Besides a screen reader, what are some of the best tools for building software with limited vision?

- Does your company employ blind engineers? How well does it work? What kind of engineer are they?

I'm really trying to get ahead of this thing and prepare myself as my vision is degrading rather quickly. I'm not sure what I can do if I can't do SE as I don't have any formal education in anything. I've worked really hard to get to where I am and don't want it to go to waste.

Thank you for any input, and stay safe out there!

Edit:

Thank you all for your links, suggestions, and moral support, I really appreciate it. Since my diagnosis I've slowly developed a crippling anxiety centered around a feeling that I need to figure out the rest of my life before it's too late. I know I shouldn't think this way but it is hard not to. I'm very independent and I feel a pressure to "show up." I will look into these opportunities mentioned and try to get in touch with some more members of the blind engineering community.

title: Ask HN: What are some cool but obscure data structures you know about?
body:
I'm very interested in what types of interesting data structures are out there HN. Totally your preference.

I'll start: bloom filters. Lets you test if a value is definitely NOT in a list of pre-stored values (or POSSIBLY in a list - with adjustable probability that influences storage of the values.)

Good use-case: routing. Say you have a list of 1 million IPs that are black listed. A trivial algorithm would be to compare every element of the set with a given IP. The time complexity grows with the number of elements. Not so with a bloom filter! A bloom filter is one of the few data structures whose time complexity does not grow with the number of elements due to the 'keys' not needing to be stored ('search' and 'insert' is based on the number of hash functions.)

Bonus section: Golomb Coded Sets are similar to bloom filters but the storage space is much smaller. Worse performance though.

title: Ask HN: Are most of us developers lying about how much work we do?
body:
I have been working as a software developer for almost two decades. I have received multiple promotions. I make decent money, 3x - 4x my area's median salary, so I live a comfortable life. I have never been fired or unemployed for more than a few months total over my entire career. Through most of that time I have averaged roughly 5 - 10 hours of actual work a week. I'm not even discounting job related but non-coding time as not work. There are literally days in which the only time I spend on my job is the few minutes it takes to attend the morning stand-up. Then I successfully bullshit my way through our next stand-up to hide my lack of production.

No one has ever called me out on this and my performance reviews range from mediocre to great. I'm generally a smart person. I went to a top 30 university, but it's not like I'm a genius or I'm coasting off connections made while getting a Harvard education. I wouldn't consider myself an abnormally talented developer. I often don't understand the technical details other engineers discuss in meetings. I have probably bombed more tech interviews than I have passed. All my jobs have been between 2-5 years so I'm neither finding a place to stagnate or leaving before anyone could judge my production. It feels like I am in the middle of the bell curve in terms of career success. So what gives?

title: Launch HN: Promise (YC W18) – Cost-effective, more humane alternative to jail
body:
Hi HN,

We are Phaedra and Diana of Promise (http://joinpromise.com/). We provide a cost-effective, more humane alternative to incarceration.

We work for government agencies to monitor and support individuals who would otherwise be in jail or who are under some form of community supervision.

There are almost 2.3 million people behind bars in the US and another 4.5+ million people on probation or parole. Almost 450,000 people are in jails pretrial, meaning they have not been convicted of the crime for which they were arrested. The majority of these individuals remain in custody because they cannot afford to pay for their release. This is costly for governments and devastating for the individuals who remain in jail who can lose their job, housing, children and more while incarcerated. Believe it or not, many of these people never even end up being charged with or convicted of a crime.

title: Helm chart: allow webhook lifecycle (preStop) and terminationGracePeriodSeconds to avoid refused admission calls during drains
body: **Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.** During a node drain or a rolling restart, the API server can still dial a terminating webhook pod for a few hundred milliseconds after the pod has stopped listening. Admission calls dialled in that gap fail: ``` failed calling webhook "validate.externalsecret.external-secrets.io": failed to call webhook: Post "https://external-secrets-webhook.external-secrets.svc:443/validate-external-secrets-io-v1-externalsecret?timeout=5s": dial tcp <pod-ip>:10250: connect: connection refused ``` Kubernetes starts removing the endpoint and sends SIGTERM at the same time, with nothing ordering the two ([pod termination](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-termination/)). The webhook cancels its context as soon as SIGTERM arrives (`cmd/controller/webhook.go`), and controller-runtime's server closes its listener first. The API server does not retry admission calls, so a GitOps dry-run (Flux, Argo CD) or an `kubectl apply` fails. This happens even with `replicaCount: 2` and the PDB enabled. We hit it on EKS 1.34 during a Karpenter drift roll. We also reproduced it on demand: we sent ~35 dry-run creates per second while deleting one of two webhook pods, and 1 of 5 deletions produced 3 refused calls about 1s after the delete. cert-manager measured the same gap at 0.3–0.4s (cert-manager/cert-manager#9590). **Describe the solution you'd like** Let the chart set the webhook's container `lifecycle` and the pod's `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, for example: ```yaml webhook: lifecycle: preStop: sleep: seconds: 10 terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30 ``` The native `sleep` action runs in the kubelet, so it works with the distroless image (GA in Kubernetes 1.34, beta and on by default since 1.30). The default could stay empty. Optionally, a built-in `--shutdown-delay` on the webhook would also fix it, like Gatekeeper's (open-policy-agent/gatekeeper#3780, default 10s) and the one cert-manager has proposed…

It was not the main daemon, which stayed up through both. ``` Nov 16 00:37:36 kernel: Out of memory: Killed process 3862121 (loom-daemon) total-vm:28808992kB, anon-rss:27617252kB Nov 17 15:08:10 kernel: oom-kill:constraint=CONSTRAINT_NONE,...,global_oom,task_memcg=/user.slice/user-1000.slice/user@1000.service/app.slice/loom-daemon.service,task=loom-daemon Nov 17 15:08:10 kernel: Out of memory: Killed process 3762474 (loom-daemon) total-vm:68396624kB, anon-rss:35044528kB Nov 17 15:08:08 systemd: loom-daemon.service: A process of this unit has been killed by the OOM killer. ``` Facts read on the host afterwards: - The killed task's cgroup is `loom-daemon.service` itself, so it is a `loom-daemon` subcommand or a fork of the daemon. Agent sessions run in their own `loom-agent-*` scopes. - Unit settings: `MemoryMax=infinity`, `MemoryHigh=infinity`, `OOMPolicy=continue`, `OOMScoreAdjust=200`. `MemoryPeak` was 58 GB on a 61 GB host. - `daemon.log` has no line naming pid 3762474. Only `git_spawn` children are logged with a pid-like id and `peak_rss_kib`. - Host memory telemetry (`loom.host.mem_available_bytes`, 2 h minima) never dropped below about 20 GB, so the growth was fast. - `loom-daemon status --json` measured under a `ulimit -v` cap peaked at 26 MB, so it is not that verb. - The other three workers (same version, same pool) had no OOM kill in the same 24 h. - Separately, each worker's main daemon was at 10 to 11 GB RSS after about 14 h of uptime. No earlier reading exists to say whether that is growth. ## Impact Small so far: dispatch continued and at most one step was lost per kill. The risk is that a global OOM picks something else next time (the main daemon, or a build). ## Asks 1. Find which `loom-daemon` invocation can reach tens of GB of anonymous memory. 2. title: Host shmem leak to 17 GB (unreclaimable) after `xe ... VM worker error: -12` while running OpenCL/OpenVINO on the PF (2026.10.28, kernel 7.0.14)
body: ## Summary On a Proxmox 9 host using `i915-sriov-dkms` 2026.10.28 (`xe.ko`, kernel `7.0.14-29-pve`), host `Shmem` grows to **17 GB** (of 24 GB RAM) and becomes **unreclaimable**, ending in a global OOM that kills unrelated processes (including a KVM guest). The pages are not mapped by any process (`sum of "Shmem:" in /proc/*/smaps == 0`) and are not in any tmpfs. They vanish immediately when the userspace GPU client is killed. The client is an **OpenVINO/OpenCL inference workload running on the PF's `/dev/dri/renderD128`** (immich-machine-learning Docker container inside an LXC). The leak starts ~3 s after the driver logs its only warning: ``` [114336.691483] xe 0000:00:02.0: [drm] VM worker error: -12 ``` Note: this looks different from #425 / #254 — no guest/VM uses a GPU VF here. SR-IOV is enabled (`max_vfs=7`) but all 7 VFs are bound to `vfio-pci` and idle. ## Environment - Proxmox VE 9.2.27, kernel `7.0.14-29-pve` - `i915-sriov-dkms/2026.10.28` (xe module version `2026.10.28-sriov`, built via DKMS for 7.0.14-29-pve); newer `2026.11.05` not tested yet - AZW EQ mini-PC, i5-13500H / Raptor Lake-P [UHD Graphics] `8086:a7a8`, 24 GB RAM, no dGPU - `xe`: `max_vfs=7`, `vram_bar_size=0`, `sriov_numvfs=7` - 00:02.0 = PF (`xe`), 00:02.1…00:02.7 = VFs, all `vfio-pci`, unused at the time of the incident - GPU user: immich-machine-learning (`openvino` image, OpenVINO GPU plugin, `/dev/dri` bind-mounted) in an LXC; models in use: SigLIP2 ViT-L-16-384, antelopev2 (det+rec), PP-OCRv6_medium (det+rec) - 3 KVM guests were running (VRAM 1/16/8 GB configured), 2 LXC; memory overcommit was high — but this only explains how fast the OOM was reached, not the 17 GB untraceable shmem ## Timeline (CST) ``` 20:59:55 xe 0000:00:02.0: [drm] VM worker error: -12 20:59:58 OpenVINO: clWaitForEvents -14 CL_EXEC_STATUS_ERROR_FOR_EVENTS_IN_WAIT_LIST followed by ~950,000 lines in 22 min of: [GPU] clFlush, error code: -5 CL_OUT_OF_RESOURCES 21:12:44 global OOM -> killed a KVM process 21:22:08…
